column47: The M.A. in Climate and Society is a 12-month interdisciplinary program that trains professionals and academics to understand and address the impacts of climate change and climate variability on society and the environment. The program’s unique and rigorous curriculum combines the flexibility of a graduate-level education with the breadth and depth of a professional degree. Students in the M.A. in Climate and Society program are part of the Columbia Climate School, a community of scholars and researchers dedicated to tackling the climate crisis. The core curriculum provides a scientific basis for inquiry and a foundation in management and policy. A dynamic set of electives allows students to apply a climate lens to a variety of fields and create a custom learning path to complement their specific interests and career goals. Drawing on the superb educational and research resources of Columbia University, the program provides students with the foundational knowledge and professional skills to tackle the climate crisis from all angles. Graduates go on to work in a variety of fields including risk management, policy, energy, adaptation, and sustainable business.

The Master of Science in Construction Administration program at Columbia University is designed to provide students with the essential skills and knowledge required for a successful career as a construction industry leader in the 21st century. The program integrates the management skills of a business school with the design sense of an architecture school and the planning acumen of an urban planning school with the engineering rigor of an engineering school. Graduates of the M.S. in Construction Administration program will be equipped with the knowledge and leadership skills necessary to have a positive impact on the built environment.

The curriculum is designed to combine the essential elements of the built environment with business and management coursework. Core courses provide the foundational knowledge necessary for success as a construction administrator. Focus area electives allow students to deepen their knowledge in specialized areas within the construction industry, including construction management, construction finance and development, real estate, construction technology, and public-private partnerships. A capstone project is required for graduation, allowing students to apply their knowledge to a real-world construction problem.

Graduates of the program will possess a broad understanding of the real estate development process, an in-depth knowledge of the construction process, excellent communication and negotiation skills, strong leadership and teamwork skills, and a commitment to ethical practice. They will be prepared to take on leadership roles in a variety of construction-related fields, including general contracting, construction management, real estate development, and infrastructure development. The program will produce graduates who will shape the built environment of the future for generations to come.

The program’s students are aspiring leaders who want to tackle the world’s most difficult sustainability challenges. The curriculum is a unique combination of environmental science and public policy, which are taught as an integrated whole, with a greater emphasis on science than other, more traditional MPA programs. In the summer, students begin with a specially designed curriculum of core courses in management, economics, and quantitative analysis. At the same time, they take a parallel set of courses in environmental science, which include earth science, chemistry, ecology and toxicology. In the fall and spring semesters, students complete the core requirements by studying a set of interdisciplinary case studies in the Workshop in Applied Earth Systems Policy Analysis. They also choose an area of specialization from the five following choices: Climate and Energy; Water; Food and Agriculture; Urban Systems and Sustainability; and ESG and Corporate Sustainability. Students complete their degrees with electives chosen from a wide variety of courses at SIPA, the Climate School and other graduate schools at Columbia University. MPA-ESP graduates work in the public, private and nonprofit sectors in the United States and worldwide. They hold positions in federal and state governments, international organizations, consulting firms, and nongovernmental organizations.

column2: Master of Science in Landscape Design
column38: School of Professional Studies
column47:
The Master of Science in Landscape Design (MSLD) program at Columbia GSAPP is a three-semester post-professional degree for students with a professional degree in landscape architecture, or architecture. The MSLD program aims to address the urgent and complex challenges of our time through design research. These challenges include the climate crisis, its impacts on biodiversity, resources, and environmental justice, as well as the need for alternative models of urbanization to support an equitable public realm.

The MSLD curriculum provides a unique platform for advanced design research, drawing upon the School’s leadership in urbanism and design, and leveraging its New York City location. Students develop a research- and design-based thesis during the intensive twelve-month program. The thesis is initiated in the summer studio and seminar with a focus on fieldwork and research methodologies, continues through the fall semester with a focus on advanced design and prototyping, and is finalized in the spring semester with a focus on thesis documentation and a public exhibition. The thesis sequence is supplemented with required and elective courses in history/theory, technology, and media, as well as opportunities for interdisciplinary study with the School’s other programs and the University at large.

The MSLD program takes an experimental and collaborative approach to the field of landscape architecture. It encourages students to think critically, and to push the boundaries of the discipline. Recent student theses have investigated a range of topics, including landscape representation, material ecologies, climate mitigation and adaptation, environmental justice, as well as the design of equitable public space. The program is enriched by a vibrant culture of events, lectures, and exhibitions, providing a dynamic learning environment for the next generation of landscape architects.

These may include particular literary or historical periods (e.g., the eighteenth century; the Goethezeit; modernism), genres (e.g., the novel; poetry; drama), or a specific theoretical or interdisciplinary field of inquiry (e.g., literary theory; intellectual history; philosophy and literature; visual culture; film studies; translation studies; gender studies).

Students are encouraged to take courses in other departments and programs, such as the Institute for Comparative Literature and Society, the Department of History, the Department of Philosophy, the Institute for the Study of Sexuality and Gender, and the Film and Media Studies program in the School of the Arts. Those with an interest in medieval studies can take advantage of the rich course offerings both at Columbia and, through the Inter-University Doctoral Consortium, at the CUNY Graduate Center, Fordham, the New School, NYU, Princeton, Rutgers, and Stony Brook. Students may also obtain a graduate Certificate in Comparative Literature and Society or in Feminist Inquiry.

The graduate program admits only Ph.D. candidates. Students will be awarded the M.A. and M.Phil. degrees en route to the Ph.D. We typically accept two to four graduate students per year. Classes are small, and students work closely with the faculty. For information about applying to the program, see the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences website.

The fully online 32-point Master of Arts Degree program in Adult Learning and Leadership is for professionals who want to lead and support adult learning and development in a range of organizational settings. Our program is a community of inquiry and practice, and a lab for change and innovation in how we learn, lead and develop as adults. A distinguishing feature of our program is its application-based focus where students are asked to take the ideas from their coursework and put them to use in their ongoing work. The curriculum is delivered fully online using both synchronous and asynchronous learning formats to deliver a state-of-the-art and cohort-based learning experience. Students who enroll in this program complete it in 16 months (four consecutive semesters).
As a student in the Adult Learning and Leadership program, you will:
- Learn key theories and concepts of adult learning and development
- Identify and apply key strategies for learning design and facilitation
- Develop key capabilities for leading and supporting learning including systems thinking, team development, group dynamics, giving and receiving feedback, conflict resolution, coaching and mentoring
- Develop skills for assessing, evaluating and researching learning
- Engage in an action research project that addresses a real problem of practice

The program is specifically designed to develop three key competencies:
1. a strategic perspective – the ability to create adult learning initiatives that are aligned with and supportive of larger organizational goals
2. instructional design capability – the ability to design and deliver effective adult learning programs
3. learning facilitation skills – the ability to create a safe and challenging learning environment that brings out the best in learners.
Our curriculum is structured to develop these skills and is built upon a strong academic foundation in the theory and practice of adult learning. The Master of Science in Computational Design Practices (MSCDP) is a new 3-term STEM-designated master’s degree at Columbia GSAPP that focuses on the development of new computational design approaches by which to address pressing contemporary social, cultural, and environmental challenges. From the design of buildings to cities, the discipline of architecture is increasingly influenced by a complex and high-volume flow of data. The MSCDP program educates a new generation of computational designers who can not only use but also create new computational design tools by which to understand and act on this data. The program empowers students to develop novel design workflows that harness the immense potential of computation to create more just, inclusive, and sustainable futures.

Students in the program apply advanced computational design skills to a specific “practice area” of their choosing—these can range from ecological simulation and climate-change modeling to responsive technologies, artificial intelligence, and urban analytics. Through a combination of required courses, specialized seminars, and independent research, students are empowered to engage with computation not only from a technical but also a critical and conceptual perspective. The program offers a hands-on and project-based curriculum organized around a year-long research thesis that students develop together with faculty.

The MSCDP program is open to applicants from a range of backgrounds including architecture, data science, engineering, and media arts. We welcome students who wish to augment their existing design skills with cutting-edge computational knowledge, as well as students with a strong technical background who wish to apply their work to design and the built environment. No prior programming experience is required.

column47: The Columbia MA in Anthropology is a selective, 30-credit degree program offering students the opportunity to pursue advanced training in socio-cultural anthropology. The department has two terminal MA programs: one based on our New York campus, and a second based at our Columbia Global Center in Paris. Both programs are designed for students with diverse academic and professional backgrounds who are interested in developing their analytic and research skills in the discipline. Students can choose to pursue the degree full-time over one year (two semesters), or part-time over up to four semesters. Each year, the MA programs brings together a vibrant, international cohort of recent college graduates and mid-career professionals who bring a wide range of experiences and perspectives to the classroom. Our students and alumni work in a variety of non-profit, government, and private sector positions; and some go on to pursue a Ph.D. in anthropology or a related discipline. The MA programs provide students with a strong foundation in contemporary social and cultural theory as well as in ethnographic research methods. Our distinguished faculty work with students to develop individualized courses of study tailored to their intellectual and professional goals. Students may enroll in courses in other Columbia departments and schools, and may also take courses in other universities through the Inter-University Doctoral Consortium.

column47: The M.A. Program in Anthropology and Education provides students with a strong grounding in anthropological theories and methods for the study of education in a wide range of settings. The program takes a broad and comparative perspective on education, and our students engage in coursework that encompasses a wide variety of topical and regional interests. Among the key strengths of our program are: courses in the social and cultural contexts of education in urban areas; issues of race, class, and gender in schooling; language, culture, and education; and migration and education in transnational contexts.

column47: The doctoral program in Mathematics Education is intended for persons who show promise of becoming leaders in the local, national, and international mathematics education community. The Ph.D. program requires a minimum of 75 graduate credits, of which at least 45 must be taken at Teachers College. The program of study for each student is planned on an individual basis. Each student is expected to develop a general knowledge of the different areas of mathematics education, to gain specialized knowledge in at least one area, and to obtain a broad understanding of related fields of inquiry. In particular, each student's program must include courses in mathematics education, mathematics, and other areas of education. All doctoral students are required to participate in a research apprenticeship for at least two semesters, working with a faculty member on one of his or her research projects. Also, all students are required to take an active part in the departmental seminars, a weekly colloquium where faculty, students, and visitors present their current work in an informal setting. A certification examination in two parts is required for the Ph.D. degree. The first part, on mathematics, is usually taken at the beginning of the second year of study. The second part, on mathematics education, is taken when the student has completed most of his or her coursework. Upon completion of the coursework and certification examinations, the student, with his or her advisor, forms a dissertation committee and prepares a dissertation proposal. The final requirement for the Ph.D. degree is the successful completion and defense of a dissertation. The dissertation must be a substantial piece of original research that makes a significant contribution to the field of mathematics education.

It is a program that combines broad coverage of literary history with a timely engagement with theoretical and interdisciplinary concerns. While the department has traditional strengths in English and American literary history, students' interests are various, ranging over all the periods of English and American literary history and including literary theory, gender studies, post-colonialism, cultural studies, and African-American studies. In all these areas, the faculty has unusual distinction and depth. A number of the faculty are associated with the School of Criticism and Theory, and with the various centers and institutes on campus, such as the Institute for Research on Women, Gender, and Sexuality, the Institute for Research in African-American Studies, the Institute for Comparative Literature and Society, the Center for the Study of Ethnicity and Race, and the Heyman Center for the Humanities.

column2: PhD in Geology and Earth Science
column38: Graduate School of Arts and Sciences
column47: The Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences (DEES) at Columbia University is an internationally recognized leader in the earth sciences. At DEES, we believe that the future of our planet depends on a deeper understanding of the earth. We use the tools of basic science to study the planet, from its core to its atmosphere, and to understand its past, present, and future. Through research, education, and outreach, we seek to advance our understanding of the earth and to share this knowledge for the benefit of all people. We are a diverse and welcoming community of scientists with a wide array of expertise and interests. Our department is part of the Columbia Climate School and is the home department for the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, one of the world's leading research centers devoted to the study of the earth. The department’s areas of strength include solid earth geophysics (seismology, geodynamics, marine geophysics, and rock mechanics), geochemistry (low-temperature, high-temperature, and isotope), oceanography (physical and chemical), paleoclimatology and paleoceanography, climate science, atmospheric science, geobiology, and environmental science. A special focus exists for the study of climate change, both past and future. The graduate program prepares students for careers in research and teaching. Many PhD students continue their studies as postdoctoral scholars and then go on to faculty or research positions at universities or research institutions such as Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. Others pursue careers in environmental consulting, the energy and mining industries, finance, and other fields.

Our program admits a small number of students each year, which enables us to provide our students with a great deal of individual attention. Columbia’s Slavic Department has long been known for its particular strengths in nineteenth- and twentieth-century Russian literature, and we continue to excel in these areas. The department is also developing a growing strength in the study of film and media. We are known for our strong culture of comparativism and our commitment to interdisciplinary inquiry, and our graduate students frequently work with faculty from a wide array of other departments, including English and Comparative Literature, History, Religion, Art History, and the Harriman Institute. We believe that clinical practice should be evidence-based and informed by the latest research, and that research should be clinically relevant and informed by the complexities of clinical practice. Our program offers excellent training in research and clinical work with a wide range of populations. Our graduates go on to work in a variety of settings, including academia, hospitals, community mental health centers, and private practice. We are committed to fostering a diverse and inclusive environment in which all students can thrive. We believe that a diverse student body enriches the learning environment and prepares our students to work with a diverse range of clients. We are also committed to social justice and to using psychology to make a positive impact on the world.

The Master of Science in Building Science and Technology (MS-BST) is an advanced research-based degree that educates students to become experts in building sciences and technology. The program offers a platform for developing fundamental knowledge and acquiring skills for research in building sciences and technologies. Students develop research methods for scientific inquiry, design experimental research, build prototypes, and learn to operate advanced equipment. They graduate with deep knowledge of building science, technology, and research methods.

The curriculum requires students to focus on a particular area of building science and develop a thesis. The study areas include building envelope, thermal performance, moisture transport, passive house design and construction, building materials, material science, advanced manufacturing and construction, building structures, structural design, structural optimization, robotics, building systems, mechanical systems, sustainable technologies, energy conservation, daylighting, lighting, water conservation, and building performance simulation and analysis. The thesis can be in the format of a research paper ready for submission to a peer-reviewed academic journal or a proof-of-concept for a technology, material, or product with commercialization potential.

Students have access to the building science and technology laboratories at GSAPP, which provides access to state-of-the-art equipment for environmental simulation, building performance analysis, and development of building systems and materials. Students work closely with the faculty on their thesis topics and research projects. With the knowledge and experience gained in the MS-BST program, graduates are qualified to develop a career in research, industry, or pursue a PhD degree.

This program introduces students to the core concepts of the anatomical sciences, including human gross anatomy, microscopic anatomy, developmental anatomy, and neuroanatomy. All courses include lecture and laboratory components, and the human gross anatomy course includes a full-body dissection.

In addition to our core curriculum, students will participate in a one-year journal club in which they learn how to read, present, and analyze primary anatomical literature. column47: The Master of Science in Real Estate Development (MSRED) program is a three-semester program that combines the fundamental skills of professional real estate with a holistic approach to urban development as a creative act. The program is cross-disciplinary, drawing on its proximity to the other programs at Columbia GSAPP and to the University at large, and it is international, with a broad vision of the real estate industry and the built environment. The program’s core curriculum gives students a shared experience, while the selection of electives allows each student to pursue his or her own particular interests. Full-time faculty members serve as advisors to all students and they guide them in shaping a course of study at GSAPP and at the University. Each of the three semesters consists of a required, interdisciplinary, and international Real Estate Development Studio. Each studio brings together all the aspects of the curriculum and applies them to a particular project. This core of the program is supported by a number of required core courses and by a selection of elective courses.

The M.A. in Climate and Society is a 12-month interdisciplinary Master of Arts program that trains professionals and academics to understand and cope with the impacts of climate variability and climate change on society and the environment. The program is offered by the Columbia Climate School, in partnership with the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

Drawing on the unparalleled educational and research resources of Columbia University, the Climate and Society program provides a unique educational experience. Our students come from a wide variety of backgrounds, but they share a common goal: to tackle the climate crisis.

A defining feature of the program is its interdisciplinary scope. Our students gain a solid foundation in climate science and learn to apply that knowledge to real-world decision-making. The curriculum is designed to be completed in 12 months, and is composed of five core courses, five electives and a summer internship or research. Students are trained to critically assess and apply climate information at various timescales, from seasonal forecasts to multi-decadal projections of climate change. Electives are chosen from a wide range of courses offered across the University, allowing students to tailor their studies to their interests. Popular areas of study include food systems, water management, environmental policy, and energy.

Our students are prepared for careers in government, business, non-profits and academic research. They benefit from a dedicated professional development team that organizes workshops, career fairs, and networking events, as well as an active and engaged alumni network.

column47:
The Master of Arts in Linguistics, Interpretation, and Translation at Columbia’s School of Professional Studies offers a comprehensive and flexible curriculum that blends academic rigor with practical application, empowering students to excel as interlingual communication professionals in diverse global settings. The program is designed for students seeking advanced training in linguistics, interpretation, and translation, as well as for those looking to transition into these fields.
The M.A. in Linguistics, Interpretation, and Translation is meticulously structured around three core pillars: linguistics, interpretation, and translation. This tripartite approach ensures a deep and holistic understanding of language and communication, preparing students for the multifaceted challenges of the global linguistic landscape.
- Linguistics forms the theoretical backbone of the program, offering students a profound understanding of language structure, meaning, and use. This foundation is crucial for mastering the nuances of interpretation and translation.
- Interpretation studies focus on the practical skills of consecutive and simultaneous interpreting, equipping students with the cognitive and technical abilities to facilitate real-time, cross-lingual communication in various professional contexts, including legal, medical, and conference settings.
- Translation studies delve into the art and science of rendering written text from one language to another, emphasizing not just linguistic accuracy but also cultural and contextual appropriateness. The curriculum covers a wide range of genres, from literary and technical texts to commercial and legal documents.
Students can customize their learning journey by selecting one of the three areas of specialization: Linguistics, Interpretation, or Translation. This flexibility allows them to tailor their studies to their specific career goals and interests, whether they aspire to be linguists, professional interpreters, or translators. The program culminates in a capstone project or a master’s thesis, providing an opportunity for students to apply their knowledge and skills to a real-world problem or an in-depth research question.
Through a blend of theoretical coursework, hands-on practice, and a final capstone or thesis, graduates of the program are well-prepared for a variety of careers in the language industry, academia, government, and the private sector. They emerge as skilled linguists, interpreters, and translators, ready to bridge communication gaps and foster understanding in an increasingly interconnected world.

column47: The Master of Science in Data Science allows students to apply data science techniques to their field of interest. Describe the major chemical, physical, and biological agents that are the basis for human disease, and understand the transport and transformation of agents in the environment and the routes of human exposure. Understand the mechanisms of toxicity for the major classes of environmental chemicals and the major disease processes that result from these exposures, including cancer, developmental and reproductive toxicity, neurotoxicity, and immune system toxicity. Understand the structure of regulatory agencies and the legal framework for environmental protection at the federal, state, and local level.

column38: Columbia Business School
column47: The Columbia Business School Executive MBA (EMBA) Program is for professionals who want to become exceptional leaders while continuing to advance their careers. Through our curriculum, you’ll gain a higher-level perspective and the ability to apply what you’ve learned immediately. We offer several scheduling options to accommodate your personal and professional needs. The EMBA program has the same core curriculum as the full-time MBA program, but is structured to provide an unparalleled experience for those who need to remain in the workforce. Students learn from world-renowned faculty at the very center of business and have access to the same resources as all other students, including career services, student clubs, and our incredible alumni network.

column47: The Dual MBA/Executive MS in Engineering and Applied Science program is a 20-month graduate curriculum that provides a unique integration of business and engineering coursework. Graduates earn two degrees: an MBA from Columbia Business School and an MS from Columbia's Fu Foundation School of Engineering and Applied Science (SEAS). MBAxMS students learn the fundamental principles of both business and engineering and gain an in-depth understanding of how to manage technology-driven organizations. Students complete the core curriculum of both programs and then have the flexibility to tailor their experience by choosing from a wide range of electives. The program is specifically designed for students who have an undergraduate degree in a STEM-related field and an interest in applying that knowledge to business.
